summary: Describes the DES-CBC cipher transform for the IP Encapsulating Security Payload, specifying how DES in cipher block chaining mode encrypts the payload. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Which scrambling method to use inside the ESP locked box, here an old coding method named DES.

questions: what is the esp des-cbc transform
how does des-cbc work with esp
what is an initialization vector in esp
subtitle: How ESP scrambles IP payloads with DES in cipher block chaining mode, and why even the authors doubted it was strong enough.

tldr.problem: The IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) needs a concrete encryption algorithm so that two implementations can actually interoperate.
tldr.mechanism: The payload is padded to a multiple of eight octets, given a Pad Length and Payload Type, and encrypted with DES in CBC mode using a per-datagram Initialization Vector that travels in the clear next to the Security Parameters Index.
tldr.outcome: Every ESP implementation that claims conformance MUST support it, but the RFC itself warns that DES is not a good algorithm for even moderately valuable data and suggests Triple DES.

today: RFC 1829 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself cautions that DES is weak for anything but low-value data and suggests Triple DES, so read it as the 1995 baseline for RFC 1827 ESP rather than a current recommendation.

sections.title: What This Transform Does
sections.content:
The Encapsulating Security Payload (RFC 1827) provides confidentiality for IP datagrams by encrypting the payload data. RFC 1829 describes how ESP uses the Cipher Block Chaining (CBC) mode of the US Data Encryption Standard (DES).

All implementations that claim conformance with the Encapsulating Security Payload specification MUST implement this DES-CBC transform, so it acts as the baseline every ESP implementation shares. The reader is assumed to know the security architecture in RFC 1825.
sections.plainLanguage: ESP is a locked box for messages. This document says every locked box must at least be able to use one particular kind of lock, called DES-CBC, so two boxes can always talk to each other.

sections.title: Keys, IVs and Data Size
sections.content:
The secret DES key shared by the two parties is eight octets long. It holds a 56-bit quantity used by the algorithm. The least significant bit of each octet is a parity bit, so the 56-bit key is stored as a 64-bit value.

CBC needs an Initialization Vector (IV), which for this mode is eight octets long. Each datagram carries its own IV, so a receiver can decrypt a datagram even when other datagrams are dropped or reordered. How IV values are chosen is implementation dependent. The RFC notes that a counter starting at a random value is commonly acceptable, though cryptanalysis could exploit the rare case where a bit position in the first DES block increments in the same way. Other implementations use a pseudo-random number generator, whose period should be long enough to avoid repetition during the lifetime of the session key.

DES works on blocks of eight octets, so the payload often needs padding. Input and output have the same number of octets, which allows in-place encryption. If the data to be decrypted is not a whole multiple of eight octets, an error is indicated as described in RFC 1825.
sections.plainLanguage: The secret key is like a shared password, and the IV is a little random starting number sent with every message. Because each message brings its own starting number, a lost letter does not stop you from reading the next one.

sections.title: The Payload Format
sections.content:
The ESP payload using this transform contains these fields in order: Security Parameters Index (SPI), Initialization Vector, Payload Data, Padding, Pad Length and Payload Type.

  • SPI: a 32-bit value identifying the security parameters for the datagram. It MUST NOT be zero.
  • IV: variable size, constant for all DES-CBC datagrams with the same SPI and IP destination. The size MUST be a multiple of 32 bits, and sizes of 32 and 64 bits must be supported. With a 32-bit field, the 64-bit IV is the 32-bit value followed by its bit-wise complement. All conformant implementations MUST also correctly process a 64-bit field.
  • Payload Data: starts with the protocol header named by the Payload Type. For IP-in-IP encapsulation (Payload Type 4) that is another IP header.
  • Padding: preferably random values, filled in before encryption to align the Pad Length and Payload Type fields. After decryption it MUST be ignored.
  • Pad Length: the size of the Padding. It typically ranges from 0 to 7 but may be up to 255 to hide the actual data length.
  • Payload Type: the IP Protocol/Payload value of the contents. For tunnel mode, encrypting an entire IP datagram, it is 4.

The Pad Length and Payload Type fields are opaque: they are set before encryption and examined only after decryption.

Even with a full 64-bit IV, the session key SHOULD be changed at least as frequently as 2**32 datagrams.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message is an envelope with a label saying which secret code to use, a starting number, the scrambled message, some filler so it fits the box size, and a note saying how much filler there is and what kind of message is inside.

sections.title: Encryption and Decryption
sections.content:
In DES-CBC, the base DES function is applied to the XOR of each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block to give the ciphertext of the current block. This also lets the receiver re-synchronize when datagrams are lost.

To encrypt, the sender appends zero or more octets of padding so that the plaintext length modulo 8 equals 6 (for a 41-octet plaintext, 5 octets of padding). It then appends a Pad Length octet and a Payload Type octet, takes an IV of the size indicated by the SPI, and encrypts with DES in CBC mode to get ciphertext of the same length. Finally it builds an IP datagram with the SPI, IV and payload. The length in the encapsulating IP header covers the encrypted data plus the SPI, IV, padding, Pad Length and Payload Type octets.

To decrypt, the receiver removes the SPI and uses it as an index into its local Security Parameter table to find the negotiated parameters and key. The negotiated form of the IV gives its size, from which a 64-bit IV is built. The payload is decrypted, then the Payload Type is examined; if it is unrecognized, the payload is discarded with an appropriate ICMP message. The Pad Length is used to strip the padding and adjust the length, and the remaining data goes to the protocol receive routine named by the Payload Type.
sections.plainLanguage: Each block of the message is mixed with the scrambled version of the block before it, like a chain where every link depends on the one before. The receiver undoes the scrambling with the shared key, throws away the filler and hands the message to the right program.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the quality of the security depends completely on the strength of DES, the correctness of its implementation, the security and implementation of key management, the strength of the key, and the correctness of all participating nodes. Applications may wish to avoid weak keys, although the odds of picking one at random are low.

It describes a cut and paste attack on all CBC algorithms: a damaged block garbles itself and the next block when decrypted, but later blocks decrypt correctly. An attacker with legitimate access to the same key could use this to insert or replay data from other users of the same engine. The usual ICMP, TCP or UDP transport checksum can detect this but is not cryptographically strong, so user or connection oriented integrity checking is needed (RFC 1826).

At the time of writing, a differential cryptanalysis attack needed 2^47 chosen plaintext-ciphertext pairs and a linear cryptanalysis attack needed 2^43 known pairs. These were not considered practical. More worrying, a design for a cracking machine costing $1 Million could crack one key every 3.5 hours. Because IP datagrams typically begin with known or guessable header text, one or two blocks of known plaintext suffice to recover a key, and frequent key changes do not help.

The RFC concludes that DES is not a good algorithm for even moderate value information against such equipment and that Triple DES is probably a better choice. It adds that ESP DES-CBC still gives far more privacy than sending the datagram as cleartext.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors admit the lock is old and a rich, determined thief with a special machine could pick it in a few hours. It still keeps out ordinary snoopers, and a stronger lock called Triple DES would be wiser for valuable things.
